The degree of f·g is m − n
The degree of f·g is the larger of m and n
The degree of f·g is always zero
questions.answer: The degree of f·g is m + n
questions.explanation: Observation in Example 3 states the degree of f·g is m + n when degrees of f and g are m and n respectively.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: According to the Remainder Theorem in the text, what is the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x − c)?
questions.explanation: Theorem 2.2 states that the remainder on division by (x − c) is f(c).
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: Which statement is the Factor Theorem as given in the text?
options: If f(c)=0 then x−c is a factor of f(x)
If f(x) has integer coefficients then all zeros are integers
If f(c)≠0 then x−c is a factor of f(x)
If f has degree n then it has exactly n distinct real zeros
questions.answer: If f(c)=0 then x−c is a factor of f(x)
questions.explanation: Theorem 2.3 states that if f(c)=0 then x−c is a factor of f(x), and conversely.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: In Example 6 the quotient when x^5 + 5x^3 − 2x^2 + 7 is divided by x^2 + 2x + 1 is:
questions.explanation: Example 6 shows the quotient of that division is x^3 − 2x^2 + 8x − 16 with remainder 24x + 23.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: Which description matches the Rational Zero Test as stated in the unit?
options: If q=p/q (in lowest terms) is a rational zero then p divides a_0 and q divides a_n
Any rational number is a zero of a polynomial with integer coefficients
All zeros of integer-coefficient polynomials are integers
If a_0=0 then all rational zeros are zero
questions.answer: If q=p/q (in lowest terms) is a rational zero then p divides a_0 and q divides a_n
questions.explanation: Theorem 2.5 states that for integer-coefficient polynomials, if q=p/q in lowest terms is a zero then p divides the constant term a_0 and q divides the leading coefficient a_n.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: What does the Location Theorem guarantee if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs?
options: There is at least one zero of f between a and b
There are no zeros between a and b
f has a rational zero between a and b
f(a) and f(b) must be equal in magnitude
questions.answer: There is at least one zero of f between a and b
questions.explanation: Theorem 2.4 states that if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs then there is at least one zero between a and b.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: From the worked example for f(x)=x^2 + 2x − 3, what is the turning point (vertex)?
questions.explanation: Completing the square gives f(x)=−4 + (x+1)^2, so the minimum occurs at x=−1 with value −4, i.e. (−1,−4).
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: For f(x)=−x^2 − 6x − 8, what is the turning point shown in the example?
questions.explanation: Completing the square yields f(x)=1 − (x+3)^2, so the maximum occurs at (−3,1) as shown in the example.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: In the wire problem (Example 1 in Applications), what is the maximum area that a rectangle made from a 56 m wire can enclose?
questions.explanation: The solution rewrites area A=−x^2 + 28x = 196 − (x−14)^2, so the maximum value is 196 m^2 attained when x=14.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: According to the same wire example, what are the dimensions of the rectangle that give the maximum area?
questions.explanation: Setting x=14 from the maximization gives y=28−x=14, so the rectangle is 14 m by 14 m (a square).
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: Given g(x)=x^3 + 4x^2 − 3x − 18 = (x + 3)^2 (x − 2) in the text, which zero has multiplicity 2?
questions.explanation: The factor (x+3) is squared, so the zero x=−3 is of multiplicity 2 as shown in the example.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: How does the graph of an even-degree polynomial with positive leading coefficient behave for large |x| according to the observations?
options: Both ends of the graph go upward (large positive)
Left end up and right end down

questions.explanation: The observations note that when degree is even and leading coefficient positive, values become large positive and the graph goes upward both far to the right and left.

questions.question: The constant function f(x)=b with b≠0 is a polynomial function of degree zero.
questions.explanation: The note states the constant function f(x)=b (b≠0) is a polynomial function with degree zero.

questions.question: If the remainder r(x) is zero when f(x) is divided by d(x), then d(x) divides f(x) exactly.
questions.explanation: The Polynomial Division Theorem notes that when the remainder r(x)=0, d(x) divides f(x) exactly (division is exact).

questions.question: The sum of two polynomial functions is not necessarily a polynomial function.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states the sum of two polynomial functions is a polynomial function.

questions.question: A polynomial function's graph is a smooth curve with no sharp corners.
questions.explanation: The notes state that the graph of a polynomial is a smooth curve (has no sharp corner), distinguishing it from functions like |x|.

questions.question: Define the term 'leading coefficient' for a polynomial function as given in the unit.
questions.answer: The leading coefficient is the coefficient a_n of the term a_n x^n corresponding to the highest power of x in the polynomial.
questions.explanation: In the definition section the text states a_n is called the leading coefficient and a_n x^n the leading term.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: Give the domain of any polynomial function according to the text.
questions.answer: The domain of any polynomial function is the set of all real numbers.
questions.explanation: The excerpt states repeatedly that the domain of a polynomial function is all real numbers.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: List the four fundamental operations on polynomial functions mentioned in the unit contents.
questions.explanation: Section 2.2 and the Unit Contents list the four fundamental operations as addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of polynomials.

questions.question: Give a one-sentence statement of the Polynomial Division Theorem as in the text.
questions.answer: If f(x) and d(x) are polynomials with d(x)≠0 and deg d ≤ deg f, then there exist unique polynomials q(x) and r(x) such that f(x)=d(x)q(x)+r(x) with r(x)=0 or deg r < deg d.
questions.explanation: Theorem 2.1 states existence and uniqueness of q(x) and r(x) with the remainder of degree less than the divisor or zero.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: State the Remainder Theorem in one sentence.
questions.answer: If f(x) is divided by (x − c) then the remainder is f(c).
questions.explanation: Theorem 2.2 shows that evaluating f at c gives the remainder upon division by x−c because (c−c)q(c)=0 leaves the constant remainder.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: What does it mean for a zero c to have multiplicity k in the polynomial f(x)?
questions.answer: It means (x−c)^k is a factor of f(x) but (x−c)^{k+1} is not, so c is a zero of multiplicity k.
questions.explanation: Definition 2.8 defines multiplicity as the exponent k such that (x−c)^k divides f(x) but (x−c)^{k+1} does not.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: Using the Factor Theorem from the unit, explain how to test whether x−c is a factor of f(x).
questions.answer: Evaluate f(c); if f(c)=0 then x−c is a factor, otherwise it is not.
questions.explanation: Theorem 2.3 states f(c)=0 implies x−c is a factor, so computing f(c) is the test.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: Summarize the Rational Zero Test procedure in one sentence.
questions.answer: List factors p of the constant term a_0 and factors q of the leading coefficient a_n, form ±p/q in lowest terms and test which values give f(q)=0 to find rational zeros.
questions.explanation: Theorem 2.5 and the listed steps instruct to take factors of a_0 and a_n, form p/q candidates and check which satisfy f=0.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 2: Polynomial Functions (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: What is the degree of f(x)=−2x + 5 as given in Example 1?

questions.question: What is the leading coefficient of f(x)=3x^2 + x − 3 from Example 1?

questions.question: What is the constant term of the product (2x + 3)(3x^2 − 5x + 6) as calculated in Example 3?

questions.question: Find the two real numbers whose difference is 16 and whose product is minimum, as solved in Example 2.

questions.question: When 3x^3 − 4x^2 + b − 5 is divided by x − 2 the remainder is 10; what is b as found in the example?

questions.question: In the expression 3^4, which identifies the base and the exponent as defined in the excerpt?

questions.question: What is the value of (−3)^2 as evaluated in the excerpt examples?

questions.question: According to Law 1 in the excerpt, a^m × a^n equals which expression?

questions.question: Which formula matches Law 2 as given in the excerpt for division of powers with same base (a ≠ 0)?

questions.question: According to Definition 3.2, a^(−n) equals which of the following (for a ≠ 0)?

questions.question: For any valid base a (a>0, a≠1), what is log_a a according to the excerpt?

questions.question: What is the y-intercept of the exponential function f(x)=a^x as stated in the excerpt?

questions.question: What is the range of the logarithmic function f(x)=log_a x for a>0, a≠1 as given in the excerpt?

questions.topic: Inverse relation of exponential and logarithm

questions.question: In the decomposition p = m × 10^c with 1≤m<10, what does the excerpt call log m?

questions.question: Using the product law, what is log_3 5 + log_3 8 equal to according to the excerpt examples?

questions.question: What does Theorem 3.2 state about log_a(M^r) in the excerpt?

questions.question: Which horizontal line is listed in the excerpt as the horizontal asymptote for y = a^x?

questions.question: Property in the excerpt: For any a>0, a≠1, log_a 1 = 0.

questions.question: The excerpt defines a^0 as undefined for all a ≠ 0.

questions.question: According to the excerpt, the graph of y = a^x has the x-axis as a horizontal asymptote.

questions.question: The excerpt warns that log_a(MN) = (log_a M)(log_a N).

questions.question: State the definition of the logarithm log_a c = b as given in the excerpt.
questions.answer: log_a c = b if and only if a^b = c.

questions.question: Write the compound interest formula for interest compounded n times per year as given in the excerpt.

questions.question: Write the formula for the amount after t years if interest is compounded continuously (as given in the excerpt).

questions.question: What is the domain of f(x)=log_a x as stated in the excerpt?

questions.question: State the definition of a^{m/n} for natural m,n and positive a as given in the excerpt.
questions.answer: a^{m/n} = (a^{1/n})^m, i.e. the n-th root of a raised to the mth power.
questions.explanation: Definition 3.4 defines a^{m/n} as (a^{1/n})^m, meaning take the n-th root of a and then raise it to the mth power.

questions.question: State Theorem 3.1 (logarithms of products) in one sentence as in the excerpt.

questions.question: Which statement restates Theorem 5.6 from the excerpt about an inscribed angle and a central angle that intercept the same arc?
options: An inscribed angle equals half the measure of the central angle that intercepts the same arc.
An inscribed angle equals twice the central angle intercepting the same arc.
An inscribed angle and the central angle are always equal in measure.
An inscribed angle is unrelated to the central angle intercepting the same arc.
questions.answer: An inscribed angle equals half the measure of the central angle that intercepts the same arc.
questions.explanation: Theorem 5.6 in the excerpt proves that an inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle intercepting the same arc, so the first option restates the theorem.

questions.question: What does Thales' Theorem, as stated in the excerpt, assert about an angle inscribed in a semicircle?

An angle inscribed in a semicircle is 60°.
An angle inscribed in a semicircle is equal to the central angle.
An angle inscribed in a semicircle is always obtuse.
questions.answer: An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle (90°).

questions.question: Which property of a cyclic quadrilateral is given as Theorem 5.9 in the excerpt?

The product of opposite sides is constant.
Opposite angles are supplementary only if the quadrilateral is a square.

questions.question: According to Theorem 5.10 in the excerpt, the measure of an angle formed by two chords intersecting inside a circle equals which of the following?

The difference of the intercepted arcs without any factor.
Twice the measure of one intercepted arc.
The product of the intercepted arcs divided by two.
questions.answer: One half the sum of the measures of the arcs intercepted by the angle and its vertical angle.
questions.explanation: Theorem 5.10 states that an angle formed by two chords inside a circle equals one half the sum of the measures of the intercepted arcs, so the first option restates the theorem.

questions.question: Example 1 for prisms: A right triangular prism has base triangle with legs 3 cm and 4 cm and altitude 6 cm; what is its volume (in cm^3) as computed in the excerpt?
questions.explanation: The excerpt computes BA = 1/2·3·4 = 6 cm^2 and V = BA·h = 6·6 = 36 cm^3, so the volume is 36 cm^3.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 6: Solid Figures (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: From Example 4 (cylinder): A right circular cylinder has radius 3 cm and altitude 5 cm. What is its total surface area (TSA) as given in the excerpt? Express your answer using π.
questions.explanation: The excerpt computes TSA = 2π r (h + r) = (2π·3)(5+3) = 48π cm^2, so TSA = 48π cm^2.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 6: Solid Figures (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: From Example 4 (cone): A right circular cone has base diameter 8 cm and height 3 cm. What is its lateral surface area (LSA) as shown in the excerpt? Express using π.
questions.explanation: The excerpt finds r = 4 cm, l = √(3^2+4^2)=5 cm, then LSA = π r l = π·4·5 = 20π cm^2.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 6: Solid Figures (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: In Example 2 for frustum: A right circular cone of altitude 8 cm and base radius 6 cm is cut to form a frustum of height 4 cm. What is the lateral surface area of the frustum as computed in the excerpt? Express using π.
questions.explanation: The excerpt computes small cone r′=3 and slant heights l=10, l′=5, so LSA(frustum)=LSA(big)−LSA(small)=60π−15π=45π cm^2.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 6: Solid Figures (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: From Example 3: A frustum of a right circular cone has slant height 26 cm, base radii 22 cm and 12 cm; what is its total surface area (TSA) in terms of π as given in the excerpt?
questions.explanation: The excerpt finds LSA = 26π(22+12)=884π and BA = π(22^2+12^2)=628π, giving TSA = 884π+628π = 1512π cm^2.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 6: Solid Figures (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: Example 4 computes the volume of a frustum whose top and bottom diameters are 6 m and 10 m and height 12 m. What is the volume in cubic metres as given in the excerpt (use the numeric value shown)?
questions.explanation: The excerpt computes r=3, r′=5 and V = 1/3 π·12(3^2+5^2+3·5)=196π ≈ 196×3.14 = 615.44 m^3, so the volume is 615.44 m^3.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 6: Solid Figures (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: Using the sphere formula given in the excerpt, what is the surface area of a sphere of radius 10 cm? Express using π.
questions.explanation: Using SA = 4π r^2 from the excerpt and r = 10 cm gives SA = 4π·10^2 = 400π cm^2.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 6: Solid Figures (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

questions.question: In Example 2 (composed solid): A solid made of a cone of altitude 3 cm on top of a cylinder of radius 4 cm has overall height 10 cm. What is the total volume of the solid as given in the excerpt (express using π)?
questions.explanation: The excerpt computes cylinder volume π·4^2·7 = 112π and cone volume 1/3 π·4^2·3 = 16π, so total = 112π+16π = 128π cm^3.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook, Unit 6: Solid Figures (owner-connected Google Drive file 1MR1DGORWmpf10Z6KiVkMm04CxfgDQ0C8).

Sunlight reaches the ground nearly vertically and it is very warm with high humidity
Extreme seasonal temperature variations like the temperate zone
Polar night conditions part of the year

Because subtropics receive the highest radiation in summer and relatively less moisture
Because subtropics have polar night conditions
Because subtropics have permanently low air pressure year-round
questions.answer: Because subtropics receive the highest radiation in summer and relatively less moisture
questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the subtropics receive high summer radiation and less moisture (e.g., due to trade winds), which contributes to desert formation in this zone.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Geography Student Textbook, Unit 2: Climate of Africa (owner-connected Google Drive file 1fzhjSsBXzQ_RfmAUm8TfViZfPKLCpWWa).

Different plants exhibit different stages of growth at the same time due to absence of climatic season
Some species of trees are xerophytic – adapted to dry environment with small leaves and thorns
Trees have little undergrowth as canopies prevent light penetration

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: If about 60 percent of jobs are in the informal or grey economy as stated in the excerpt, what percent of jobs are not in the informal or grey economy?

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: Express the excerpt's figure '21%' (Africa's share of the world's projected urban population) as a decimal.

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: The excerpt states Africa's urban population is expected to reach 2.5 billion in 2050 and that this accounts for 21% of the world's projected urban population; calculate the world's projected urban population (in billions) implied by these figures. Give your answer rounded to one decimal place.

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: Using the excerpt's statement that about 60 percent of jobs are in the informal economy, express the ratio of informal to formal jobs in simplest whole-number form.

questions.question: In the Teso community case study presented, remains were exhumed from graves that were at least how many years old?

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: Define 'unplanned urbanization' as described in the excerpt.
questions.answer: Unplanned urbanization is urban expansion and population growth that occur in an unregulated, random or unexpected way, leading to environmental damage and inadequate services.
questions.explanation: The excerpt explains unplanned urbanization involves unregulated growth that damages the environment and outpaces planning and infrastructure, which the answer summarizes.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Geography Student Textbook, Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa (owner-connected Google Drive file 1fzhjSsBXzQ_RfmAUm8TfViZfPKLCpWWa).

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: Provide the definition of 'migration' given in the excerpt.
questions.answer: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to establish permanent or semi-permanent residence at the destination.
questions.explanation: The excerpt defines migration as movement of people to establish permanent or semi-permanent residence at a destination, which the answer restates.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Geography Student Textbook, Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa (owner-connected Google Drive file 1fzhjSsBXzQ_RfmAUm8TfViZfPKLCpWWa).

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: In your own words, define 'urban primacy' as used in the excerpt.
questions.answer: Urban primacy is the condition where one city, usually the capital, has population, economic activity and political power several times greater than the next largest city.
questions.explanation: The excerpt defines urban primacy exactly as one dominant city far larger in population and power than the next city, which the answer reflects.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Geography Student Textbook, Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa (owner-connected Google Drive file 1fzhjSsBXzQ_RfmAUm8TfViZfPKLCpWWa).

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: Define 'slum' or 'squatter settlement' as described in the excerpt.
questions.answer: A slum or squatter settlement is an unlawful residential area that develops from random, unexpected urban growth where residents lack adequate services and secure land tenure.
questions.explanation: The excerpt describes slums and squatters as unlawful residential settlements arising from unplanned growth, often with poor services and tenure insecurity, which the answer summarizes.
questions.sourceNote: Grade 10 Geography Student Textbook, Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa (owner-connected Google Drive file 1fzhjSsBXzQ_RfmAUm8TfViZfPKLCpWWa).

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa
questions.question: List the causes of unplanned urbanization in Africa cited in the excerpt (give up to five).
questions.answer: Unplanned and unregulated growth; the legacy of colonialism; structural adjustment programs of international institutions (e.g., IMF); pressure from developed countries (neoliberal policies); weak urban planning institutions.

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa

questions.answer: Transportation infrastructure is very weak; water supply and sewage are in serious shortage.
questions.explanation: The Focus box on urban infrastructure lists weak transportation systems and serious shortages in water supply and sewage as characteristics, which the answer cites.

questions.unitTitle: Unit 7: Geographic Issues and Public Concerns in Africa

questions.answer: They result in adaptation responses which are implementation actions to respond to environmental impacts that have already occurred as well as future impacts.

questions.answer: They apply equally to all people everywhere and are not time-limited.
questions.explanation: Universalism means human rights apply equally to all people everywhere, with no time limit, while respecting diversity.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: When, according to the text, do individuals stop enjoying their human rights?
options: When they move to another country
questions.explanation: Eternality means individuals enjoy their human rights until the time of natural death.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which statement best captures the inalienability of human rights as explained in the unit?
options: They can be permanently taken away by the state during emergencies.
They are inherent to human existence, though some may be lawfully restricted in specific circumstances.
They apply only if a person has not committed a crime.
They can be traded for other legal privileges.
questions.answer: They are inherent to human existence, though some may be lawfully restricted in specific circumstances.
questions.explanation: Inalienability means rights are inherent to all humans; some can be suspended or restricted in particular situations (e.g., curfew in emergencies, loss of liberty after conviction).
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which example from the text illustrates the indivisible and interdependent nature of human rights?
options: Economic rights can be enjoyed without civil rights.
Rights are ranked so that some are more important than others.
Progress in civil and political rights makes it easier to exercise economic, social and cultural rights.
Violations of social rights do not affect other rights.
questions.answer: Progress in civil and political rights makes it easier to exercise economic, social and cultural rights.
questions.explanation: The unit explains that rights are intrinsically connected; advancing one set (civil and political) facilitates others (economic, social, cultural).
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: What does the inviolability of human rights imply according to the lesson?
options: They may be routinely limited by private actors.
They are expected not to be violated or even restricted by anyone.
They can be overridden to promote cultural uniformity.
They apply only in stable times, not during crises.
questions.answer: They are expected not to be violated or even restricted by anyone.
questions.explanation: The text states that by their nature human rights are expected not to be violated or even restricted, with some countries extending this logic even during emergencies.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: In this unit, what is meant by human rights being irrevocable?
options: They can be repealed by majority vote.
They cannot be taken away by any power or authority.
They are temporary privileges during emergencies.
They are negotiable based on social status.
questions.answer: They cannot be taken away by any power or authority.
questions.explanation: Human rights are described as irrevocable because they originate from the social nature of humans and belong to a person simply for being human.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which of the following is identified in the text as a first generation (civil and political) right?
options: Freedom from torture and from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment
Right to economic and social development
questions.answer: Freedom from torture and from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment
questions.explanation: First generation rights include civil and political rights such as freedom from torture, as listed in the unit.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which right is listed as a second generation (economic, social, and cultural) right?
options: Freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention
Right to participate in government through free elections
questions.explanation: Second generation rights include economic, social, and cultural rights such as the right to work and education.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which right is identified as part of the third generation of rights in the unit?
options: Right to a fair and public trial
Right to political, economic, social, and cultural self-determination
Right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being
questions.answer: Right to political, economic, social, and cultural self-determination
questions.explanation: The third generation includes rights such as self-determination and the right to development, as described in the text.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: What does the lesson state about universality and cultural diversity?
options: Universality does not threaten diversity and allows states to define higher standards.
Diversity is incompatible with equal human rights.
Universalism applies only to civil rights, not social rights.
questions.answer: Universality does not threaten diversity and allows states to define higher standards.
questions.explanation: The text clarifies that universality is not synonymous with uniformity and that states may apply higher, more specific standards beyond the minimums.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which principle is expressly articulated in Article 10 of the FDRE Constitution as highlighted in the unit?
options: Human rights are granted by government discretion.
Human rights and freedoms, emanating from the nature of mankind, are inviolable and inalienable.
Only democratic rights are justiciable in courts.
Human rights apply only to citizens.
questions.answer: Human rights and freedoms, emanating from the nature of mankind, are inviolable and inalienable.
questions.explanation: The unit quotes Article 10 stating that human rights and freedoms are inviolable and inalienable because they emanate from the nature of mankind.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: According to the unit, which articles of the FDRE Constitution are named “Human Rights”?
questions.explanation: The text states that Articles 14–28 are named “Human Rights,” while Articles 29–44 are “Democratic Rights.”
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: According to the unit’s discussion of Article 10 of the FDRE Constitution, human rights and freedoms emanating from the nature of mankind are described as what?
questions.explanation: The narrative discussion states that Article 10 describes human rights and freedoms emanating from the nature of mankind as inviolable and inalienable.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which is identified in the lesson as an obligation of citizens in realizing human rights?
questions.explanation: The unit lists citizen obligations including respect for religious equality, gender equality, others’ rights, and the national flag.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: How should individuals exercise their rights according to the lesson?
options: Only when approved by private actors
With due regard for the rights of others
questions.answer: With due regard for the rights of others
questions.explanation: The unit states that individuals have a responsibility to exercise their rights with due regard for the rights of others and the community.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which action would violate the state’s obligation to respect human rights as explained in the unit?
options: Enacting laws against human rights abuses by private actors
Performing medical experiments on persons with disabilities without their consent
Providing impartial legal remedies for violations
Hiring more teachers to expand access to education
questions.answer: Performing medical experiments on persons with disabilities without their consent
questions.explanation: Under the obligation to respect, states must refrain from interfering with rights, including not conducting non-consensual medical experiments on persons with disabilities.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: What does the state’s obligation to protect require, according to the lesson?
options: Restricting all civil liberties during emergencies
Acting against abuses by non-state actors and ensuring access to remedies
Leaving rights enforcement to families and private groups
Focusing only on criminal law enforcement
questions.answer: Acting against abuses by non-state actors and ensuring access to remedies
questions.explanation: The obligation to protect requires the state to prevent and remedy abuses by non-state actors, enact legislation, act when aware of threats, and ensure impartial remedies.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Which measure exemplifies the state’s obligation to fulfill the right to education in the unit?
options: Reducing public schools to encourage private providers
Setting up enough public schools or hiring and remunerating adequate numbers of teachers
Allowing third parties to indoctrinate students
Excluding persons with disabilities from school on cost grounds
questions.answer: Setting up enough public schools or hiring and remunerating adequate numbers of teachers
questions.explanation: The unit states that to fulfill rights, states should take positive steps such as providing means for education, including establishing schools and hiring teachers.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Universality of human rights means all cultures must apply identical standards and practices.
questions.explanation: The text states universality means rights apply equally to all people and is not synonymous with uniformity; societies may adopt higher or more specific standards.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Second generation rights include economic, social, and cultural rights and are conceived more in positive terms that encourage state intervention.
questions.explanation: The text explains that second generation rights broaden to economic, social, and cultural rights and are conceived in positive terms, encouraging state action.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: The obligation to protect requires the State to shield individuals from abuses by non-State actors and ensure access to impartial legal remedies when violations are alleged.
questions.explanation: According to the text, the State must protect against abuses by non-State actors and provide access to impartial remedies.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) is not legally binding, yet many UN member states have incorporated its principles into their national constitutions.
questions.explanation: The text notes the UDHR is not legally binding but has been influential, with many states incorporating its principles into constitutions.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: According to the text (UDHR Article 2), what is the only criterion someone must fulfill to enjoy human rights?
questions.explanation: The text states that human rights belong to every human being without distinction and that the only criterion to enjoy these rights is being a human.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: When, in principle, do individuals stop enjoying their human rights?
questions.answer: At the time of natural death.
questions.explanation: The feature of eternality states that individuals stop enjoying their human rights only at natural death.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Name one circumstance mentioned in the text under which some human rights may be suspended or restricted.
questions.answer: During a publicly declared national emergency, a government may impose a curfew restricting freedom of movement.
questions.explanation: The text notes that in particular circumstances, such as a declared national emergency, some rights may be derogated, e.g., by imposing a curfew.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: What does it mean that human rights are “indivisible and interdependent”?
questions.answer: Rights are intrinsically connected; enjoyment of one depends on others, and no right is more important than the rest.
questions.explanation: The text explains that human rights cannot be viewed in isolation and that full enjoyment of any right depends on many others.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: In the FDRE Constitution, which articles are designated “Human Rights,” and which are “Democratic Rights”?
questions.answer: Articles 14–28 are “Human Rights”; Articles 29–44 are “Democratic Rights.”
questions.explanation: Chapter three divides Fundamental Rights and Freedoms into Human Rights (Arts. 14–28) and Democratic Rights (Arts. 29–44).
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: Give one constitutional obligation of citizens mentioned for protecting human rights.
questions.explanation: The text lists citizen obligations including respect for religious equality, gender equality, others’ rights, and the national flag.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: List the three types of state obligations toward human rights identified in the text.
questions.answer: Obligations to respect, to protect, and to fulfill.
questions.explanation: The lesson outlines that states must respect, protect, and fulfill human rights, each with distinct duties.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: What is the legal status of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights and for what purpose was it adopted?
questions.answer: It is not legally binding; it was adopted to define the “human rights” and “fundamental freedoms” referenced in UN Charter Article 55(c).
questions.explanation: The text states the UDHR is not legally binding but was adopted to define rights and freedoms that UN members must observe and respect.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: How many basic features of human rights are explicitly listed (Universalism, Eternality, Inalienability, Indivisible and interdependent, Inviolability, and that human rights are irrevocable)?
questions.explanation: The text names six features: Universalism; Eternality; Inalienability; Indivisible and interdependent; Inviolability; and that human rights are irrevocable. Counting them gives 6 features.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: How many generations of human rights are described in the lesson (first, second, and third generation rights)?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly discusses three generations: first generation rights, second generation rights, and third generation rights. Counting these gives 3 generations.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.topic: FDRE Constitution — Fundamental Rights and Freedoms span
questions.question: Articles 13–44 of the FDRE Constitution are devoted to “Fundamental Rights and Freedoms.” How many articles does this inclusive range contain?
questions.explanation: Inclusive count: 44 − 13 + 1 = 32 articles.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: How many articles are named “Human Rights” in the FDRE Constitution (Articles 14–28 inclusive)?
questions.explanation: Inclusive count: 28 − 14 + 1 = 15 articles.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.question: How many articles are dubbed “Democratic Rights” in the FDRE Constitution (Articles 29–44 inclusive)?
questions.explanation: Inclusive count: 44 − 29 + 1 = 16 articles.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.topic: UDHR ranges cited for first and second generation rights
questions.question: Across the UDHR article ranges cited for first (Articles 2–21) and second (Articles 22–27) generation rights, how many UDHR articles are covered in total?
questions.explanation: First range count: 21 − 2 + 1 = 20 articles. Second range count: 27 − 22 + 1 = 6 articles. Total: 20 + 6 = 26 articles.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.1 The concept of human right, printed pp. 126–131 (owner-approved local source).

questions.topic: State obligations in realizing human rights
questions.question: How many distinct types of state obligations to realize human rights are identified (obligation to respect, protect, and fulfill)?
questions.explanation: The text lists three obligations: obligation to respect; obligation to protect; obligation to fulfill. Counting them gives 3 obligations.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).

questions.topic: State obligation to fulfill — education measures
questions.question: Under the obligation to fulfill the right to education, how many distinct education-related provisions are listed (free and compulsory primary education for all; free secondary education; higher education; vocational training; adult education; elimination of illiteracy)?
questions.explanation: Enumerated provisions: (1) free and compulsory primary education for all; (2) free secondary education; (3) higher education; (4) vocational training; (5) adult education; (6) elimination of illiteracy. Count = 6 items.
questions.sourceNote: Citizenship Education Student Textbook, Grade 10, Unit 6, §6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights, printed pp. 132–135 (owner-approved local source).
